Three reasons people wait, and what the book says to each.

“AI is overhyped.”The Mirror Principle: AI reflects the quality of your direction (Ch 1).+

The model has no goals of its own, so it mirrors back what you bring. The book's image is a lamp against a beam: a vague prompt lights the whole room, and a precise one narrows the beam onto the thing you need. A flat answer usually tells you the brief was thin, and a brief can be fixed.

“I'm not technical.”The skill is direction, and you already use it at work (Ch 3).+

The Director's Mindset puts you in the chair with AI as the crew. You supply the judgment, the direction and the check, which is what you already do when you hand work to a colleague.

Priya, a consultant in the book (a character, a composite), practised for two weeks in January and had twelve templates by March, and “no technical training went into any of it.”

“The tools change too fast.”A good brief carries over from one model to the next (Ch 6).+

ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini share the same engine underneath, and each one mirrors the quality of what you type. In the book's words, “The skill you're building here transfers to every tool, because the underlying engine is the same one.” Product names will keep changing, and your briefs keep working.

The method

AI mirrors the brief you give it. Build one now.

This is the three-part brief from Chapter 3. Fill it in for a task on your desk this week.

“A vague prompt covers ground the way a lamp covers a room. A precise one narrows the beam to a point.”

Adapted from Chapter 1

Three boxes, one brief. Nothing you type leaves this page.

Your brief

Act as a chief of staff who writes for busy executives. Turn my notes below into a weekly update for my director. Lead with the one decision I need, three bullets at most, under 120 words.

That's one framework. Chapter 3 teaches the rest of the brief, and Chapter 11 shows you how to fix the draft when it misses.

Marcus is a character from the book, a composite

Marcus closed the tab for two months. Then he learned to brief it.

  1. Ch 3One bad first tryHe typed a vague question and got a generic list.+

    Marcus managed product launches at a mid-sized software company. He typed “best go-to-market strategy for B2B SaaS” and got a list he could have found on any marketing blog. He didn't open the tool again for two months.

  2. Ch 3Three minutes of directionA colleague nudged him back, and he tried a proper brief.+

    He gave the model his product, his timeline, his team size and the two obstacles his sales team kept hitting. He brought the working first draft to leadership that afternoon.

  3. Ch 14A library that growsSix months in, he had fourteen saved templates.+

    Product launches stopped feeling hard, and his manager started handing him the cross-functional problems that tend to come before a promotion. Each saved template made the next task faster.

  4. Ch 15Senior DirectorPromoted that spring, with a method his team copied.+

    Within six weeks of his first strategy review, his team had adapted his brief for their own work. More than twenty templates lived in a shared folder by the end of the year, and he never asked anyone to use them.

Start where Marcus started →

Your first week, then your first three months.

Chapter 14 turns what you read into a practice plan.

  1. First week · Quick-startOne real task a day, with low stakes.+

    Each workday, use AI for one task that needs doing anyway: an email, a summary, an outline or some research for a decision. Keep the stakes low enough that a mistake costs nothing. Save the first prompt that works (Ch 5 shows you how).

  2. Month 1 · Make it habitualReaching for AI becomes your default.+

    Keep one real task a day. At the end of each week, find one task you did more than once and save a template for it. You'll know it's working when you stop asking whether to use AI for something and just use it.

  3. Month 2 · Make it strategicYou can say why a good output was good.+

    Sharpen the templates that needed fixing every time. Try ranking the details that matter most and putting them first. On one complex task, ask AI to interview you before it answers.

  4. Month 3 · Make it systematicYour prompt library becomes part of how you work.+

    Organise your library by task, workflow or audience. The book pictures a Tuesday at week twelve where a request that once ate your afternoon becomes a strong draft twenty minutes later.

AI can sound certain and still be wrong. Two steps catch it.

A story from Chapter 13 about two colleagues and one confident number.

1 · Same prompt

Diana and James asked AI for a market size for the same client pitch. It came back confident, with a growth rate to the decimal.

2 · James

He pasted the number into his slide and moved on. It looked right and read right.

3 · Diana

She paused and checked where the figure came from before it went on a slide.

4 · The meeting

The client flagged James's number as outdated. He spent fifteen minutes explaining. Diana spent thirty seconds citing her source.

Diana and James are characters from the book, composites.

Step oneSort the claimIs it a fact, a judgment call or a creative draft?+

Facts can be flatly right or wrong, so that's where your checking goes. Judgment calls get your own judgment, and drafts get judged on fit.

Step twoMatch effort to stakesA glance for small things, and an expert for big ones.+

A book suggestion gets a quick look. A figure going in front of a client gets a real check. Legal, financial or medical claims go to a professional.

Waiting has a cost, and the book calls it the Foundation Tax.

“The most expensive time to learn something is right after you needed it.” Chapter 5

What the tax isThe extra cost of learning a skill after it's expected (Ch 5).+

The book defines it as “the extra cost, in time, energy, and credibility, that deferred learning charges when the environment already assumes a fluency you haven't built.” It builds slowly and then shows up all at once.

What two early weeks boughtPriya's head start came from her calendar (Ch 5, a character from the book).+

She practised for two weeks in January while the learning curve was forgiving. Within a few months she had close to two days a week back. The book's advice is to start while free tiers and patient teams still make practice cheap.

The cheapest place to start is one brief on one real task this week.

Questions people ask before they buy

Do I need a technical background?

None. The book is written for professionals with no technical training. If you can write an email, you can use everything in it.

Which AI tool does it use?

It works with ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot. Part 2 helps you pick one, and the directing skill carries over to all of them.

Will it go out of date when the tools change?

The book teaches you how to direct AI, and that skill carries over from one model to the next. The product names will keep changing, and your briefs will keep working.

I already use AI at work. Is it still for me?

Yes, if your results are hit and miss. The frameworks turn scattered habits into a method you can repeat, and the appendices give you prompts and fixes to keep beside your work.

What if AI gets something wrong?

Chapter 13 gives you a two-step check: sort the claim, then match your checking to the stakes. Appendix F covers invented facts and nine other common failures, each with a corrective prompt.

I'm a manager. Can my team use it?

Yes. Chapter 7 helps a team settle on one tool, and the saved-template habit gives everyone prompts to share. One copy per person keeps the whole team on the same method.

Can I read some of it first?

Yes. Chapter 8 is free to read, and it shows you which AI mode fits which job.
